common_name: Farthing Southern Highbush Blueberry (High-Yield Midseason Blueberry)

planting.note: Plant during winter dormancy in very acidic (pH 4.5-5.5), well-drained soil amended with pine bark; Farthing has a low chill requirement of roughly 300-350 hours and its heavy bloom benefits from a second midseason southern highbush cultivar nearby for cross-pollination and fuller berry set.

directions: Plant container-grown or dormant bare-root bushes in winter into raised, sulfur-amended beds if native soil is not already strongly acidic, and mulch with pine bark to conserve moisture through summer heat. Farthing is a University of Florida southern highbush release valued by Gulf Coast growers for its exceptionally heavy, reliable yields of medium-large, firm, light-blue berries with a mild, well-balanced flavor on a vigorous, upright bush. It ripens over a fairly long midseason window, which spreads out the harvest and makes it a strong choice for home orchards wanting an extended picking period. Feed lightly with acid-forming fertilizer in early spring and after harvest, and renewal-prune out the oldest wood each winter to sustain the heavy fruit set.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Southern Highbush Blueberry Cultivars

common_name: Camellia Southern Highbush Blueberry (Mild-Flavored Productive Blueberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes in winter in acidic, well-drained soil amended with pine bark or peat; Camellia needs about 300 chill hours, flowers early to midseason, and sets a heavier crop with a second low-chill southern highbush cultivar planted nearby.

directions: Amend planting beds to pH 4.5-5.2 with pine bark fines before setting out dormant bushes in winter, and keep roots consistently moist with a thick mulch layer since southern highbush blueberries have shallow, fibrous root systems. Camellia is a University of Florida release known for very high, consistent yields of medium to large, firm, light-blue berries with a mild, low-acid flavor that many home growers find especially easy-eating fresh off the bush. The upright, vigorous plant tends to hold its crop well without excessive splitting in Gulf Coast humidity. Prune out the oldest canes each winter to renew fruiting wood, and fertilize lightly with an acid-forming blueberry fertilizer split between early spring and shortly after harvest.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Southern Highbush Blueberry Cultivars
LSU AgCenter — Blueberry Variety Performance in Louisiana
North Carolina State Extension — Blueberry Cultivar Evaluations

common_name: Avonblue Southern Highbush Blueberry (Early Florida-Bred Blueberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes in winter in strongly acidic, well-drained soil; Avonblue is largely self-fruitful with a low chill requirement near 400 hours, but yields improve with a second low-chill southern highbush cultivar planted for cross-pollination.

directions: Set out dormant, container-grown bushes in winter into acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.2) heavily amended with pine bark or peat moss, and mulch to keep the shallow root zone cool and evenly moist. Avonblue is one of the older University of Florida southern highbush releases and remains valued for its dependable early ripening, largely self-fruitful flowers, and tolerance of Florida's sandy, warm-winter growing conditions. Berries are medium-sized, light blue, and mildly tart, produced on a moderately compact, rounded bush well suited to smaller home garden plantings. Feed with an acid-forming fertilizer in early spring, water deeply during dry spells, and prune out old unproductive wood each winter to keep the bush renewing itself.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Southern Highbush Blueberry Cultivars

common_name: Gulfcoast Southern Highbush Blueberry (Original Low-Chill Florida Blueberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes in winter in acidic, well-drained soil amended with pine bark or peat; Gulfcoast needs only about 300 chill hours, ripens early, and yields best with a second low-chill southern highbush cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Plant in raised beds or native soil amended to pH 4.5-5.2 with pine bark fines, setting out dormant bushes in winter and mulching well to protect the shallow root system from summer heat. Gulfcoast was among the first University of Florida southern highbush releases bred specifically for the state's mild winters, and it remains a reliable, vigorous producer of medium, firm, light-blue berries with good flavor on an upright, spreading bush. Its very low chilling requirement makes it dependable even after unusually warm winters along the Gulf Coast, where many northern blueberry varieties fail to set fruit. Fertilize lightly with acid-forming fertilizer in early spring, water during dry spells to support fruit sizing, and prune out old wood each winter to keep the planting productive.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Southern Highbush Blueberry Cultivars
